newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Payrolls, dollar and anxiety.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Payrolls, dollar and anxiety.

text.p: The long-awaited November employment report and the performance of the dollar against other major currencies will share the attention of battered U.S. credit markets on Friday, analysts said.
Treasury prices, which slumped almost 1-1/2 point in late trade on Thursday, are expected to open choppy as players fix their eyes to the screens ahead of the release of the payroll numbers.
The Labor Department will issue the data on Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
A recent Reuters survey showed U.S. economists expect, on average, non-farm payrolls to rise by 179,000 in November against a 210,00 rise in the previous month.
Analysts said that given the market's bearish sentiment over the last few sessions, any number above 200,000 on payrolls might spark a fresh selloff.
"If you told people now that it's going to be a 220,000 rise (in payrolls) tomorrow, that would be bad," said Chris Rupkey, vice-president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi.

Analysts said part of the sell-off on Thursday -- which brought the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond yield up to 6.50 percent, the highest since level November 8 -- was tied to unconfirmed rumors that the employment report would be stronger than the expected consensus number.
"There was some selling after the rumors hit the market ... and if we get a confirmation of those rumors tomorrow (on Friday) people might continue to sell," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Some analysts said, however, they are keeping their bullish call on the U.S. Treasury market.
"I think trading (on Thursday) was tied to a sense of denial about the deceleration in the economy," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities.
"But ironically the consensus forecast numbers (for payrolls) ... indicate continued deceleration of the pace of job growth," Levenson added.
The weakness of the dollar against major currencies has also been a factor driving Treasuries down.
Pundits fear further possible drops in the greenback exchange rate, mainly against the Japanese yen, could prompt foreign players to unwind dollar-demoninated positions.

"A lot of the recent rally on this market was tied to a steady flow of foreign money ... If those guys decide to unwind positions we might see further, continued selling here," said another trader at a foreign investment bank.
Pundits also said the recent run up in prices, which was followed by the sharp drop over the last few days, created a fuzzy picture on the charts.
They said it has been difficult to define a trend and most chart analysts are expecting to get their cues out of the market's performance on Friday.
"Let's see what the release of payrolls will do to the charts. For now it's a real fuzzy picture," the trader said.
The benchmark bond was quoted down 1-13/32 at 99-31/32 in late Thursday trade to yield 6.50 percent.

The Federal Reserve added reserves to the banking system on Thursday through four-day fixed system repurchase agreements when the federal funds were changing hands at 5-5/16 percent, above the Fed's 5-1/4 percent target.
The Fed refrained once again from adding permanent reserves to the system via an expected coupon pass operation. Funds are seen opening Friday at 5.20 percent. -- 212-859-1676
